extra_snippets: Based on Fichte's conception of international law from the Grundlage des Naturrechts the article examines to what extent a League of nations is compatible with the sovereignty of a nation state. Fichte's concept of sovereignty refers to a republican notion of a state which guaranties the congruence of power and right.

This principle leads to an internal tension, for the League presupposes the existence of sovereign states and in the same time curtails their competences. It manifests an instance of power without the legitimation of the singular nations. Fichte avoids the paradoxes of the Kantian vision of a perpetual peace, because he develops a more complex concept of political power, but it remains to be a contradictory construction.

Fichte described his conversion from Spinoza to Kantianism as turning on the acceptance of ‘the concept of absolute freedom’ and his own system of philosophy as ‘the first system of freedom’. This chapter explores the meaning and content of Fichte’s concept of ‘absolute freedom’ and the grounds on which Fichte thinks it is rational for us to believe the human will has absolute freedom.

Fichte equates absolute freedom with volition, conceived as “the free transition from determinability to determination with consciousness of the transition.” This requires both that we be the absolute source of our actions and that we have a plurality of possible actions available to us.

The grounds for belief in our freedom consists first in a commitment to morality, and second in the fact that absolute freedom is a presupposition of theoretical understanding, comprehension, and conviction. By “commitment to morality,” however, Fichte understands only action under normative concepts, and not the conditions of moral responsibility, or blame.
